conversation.content: Let's design a URL shortening service — like bit.ly. Users give us a long URL, we give back a short one that redirects. What questions do you have?
How many people will use this?
50 million new URLs per day, with a 100:1 read-to-write ratio. So 5 billion redirects per day. What else matters?
That's a lot. Um, do short URLs expire? And can people choose their own custom short URL?
Yes to both — configurable TTL with 5-year default, and optional custom aliases. Let's start with the basic design. How would you build this?

We need a database that stores the mapping from short URL to long URL. When someone submits a long URL, we generate a short code, save the mapping, and return the short URL. When someone clicks the short URL, we look up the long URL and redirect them.
Good basic flow. How do you generate the short code?
A random string? Like, generate 6 random characters from a-z and 0-9. Check if it already exists in the database. If it does, generate another one.

That could work, but with 50 million URLs per day, the collision rate will increase over time. After a year, you'll have billions of URLs and lots of collisions. Is there a way to guarantee uniqueness without checking?
Maybe use an auto-incrementing number? Like URL number 1, 2, 3, and so on. Each number is unique by definition. Then convert the number to a short string somehow.

Exactly. You can convert the number to a base-62 string (using a-z, A-Z, 0-9). The number 1000000 in base-62 is just a few characters. No collisions ever. What database would you store the mappings in?
MySQL? It's reliable and supports auto-increment for the ID generation. We'd have a table with short_code, long_url, created_at, and expires_at.
MySQL works for small scale. But 50 million writes and 5 billion reads per day — can one MySQL instance handle that?

50 million writes is about 580 per second — MySQL can probably handle that. 5 billion reads is about 58,000 per second — that's a lot for one server. Maybe add read replicas? The reads are simple lookups by short_code, so replicas can handle them.
Good math! Read replicas help. But 58,000 reads per second could be expensive. Is there something faster than a database for these lookups?

A cache? Like Redis? We could check Redis first before going to the database. Popular URLs would be in the cache and served super fast. If it's not in the cache, check the database and add it to the cache for next time.

Good — that's called cache-aside pattern. With the 80/20 rule, most traffic goes to a small fraction of URLs, so the cache hit rate would be very high. When someone clicks the short URL, do we send a 301 or 302 HTTP redirect?

I'm not sure of the difference... 301 is permanent and 302 is temporary? I think 302 is safer because if we ever need to change where the URL points, 301 would be cached by the browser and they'd never see the update.

That's a valid consideration. 302 also means every click goes through our servers, which is better for analytics — we can count clicks. 301 would be cached by the browser and we'd lose visibility. Good instinct. What happens if your Redis cache goes down?

All 58,000 reads per second hit the database directly. That might overwhelm it. We could... have the cache be a cluster with replicas so one node failing doesn't take down the whole cache? And rate limit the fallback to the database so it doesn't get crushed.
Good thinking — Redis cluster with replication is the right approach. We're almost done. Anything you'd add?

A cleanup job that deletes expired URLs. Rate limiting on the creation endpoint so people can't spam millions of short URLs. And maybe analytics — how many times each URL was clicked, from which countries.
Nice practical additions. You needed some guidance today but you picked up concepts quickly — base-62 encoding, caching, and QPS calculations. Keep building on that foundation. Thanks!

strengths: Good QPS calculation — correctly derived 580 writes/sec and 58K reads/sec from daily numbers
Picked up base-62 encoding concept quickly once introduced
Practical additions at the end — TTL cleanup, rate limiting, analytics
weaknesses: Initial encoding approach (random string with collision check) showed lack of preparation
Needed hinting for every major concept — base-62, caching, redirect types
Couldn't independently discuss database sharding or geographic distribution
Cache failure handling was shallow — mentioned clustering but didn't design the failover
Requirements gathering was minimal — only two questions
